summary: The heartbeat closes the main reported defect: a job in a long, blocking stage (convert_outputs) now re-stamps 'updated' every heartbeat_seconds() while at least one thread is alive to run it, so a slow-but-alive job is no longer declared stale mid-stage, and the delete-then-save race that could momentarily 404 a poll is fixed by an atomic os.replace on the local backend. The tests (test_heartbeat.py) exercise both halves: a live job stays RUNNING past the stale window, and a dead one (heartbeat never started, or stopped) still gets marked FAILED on read. Two gaps remain in what the commit adds: (1) the join that is supposed to guarantee the beat lands before a terminal write is bounded by a timeout, and nothing checks whether the thread actually stopped before the caller proceeds to write DONE/FAILED -- so under a slow or hung write_status (no timeouts are configured anywhere on the storage backend calls in this codebase), a straggling heartbeat write can still land after the terminal status and flip a finished/failed job back to RUNNING, which is the same false-recovery failure mode in reverse. (2) write_status swallows every exception with only a logger.warning, and the heartbeat loop does nothing to count or escalate repeated failures -- so a run of failed beats (expired credentials, throttled storage, a full local disk) silently reopens the exact false-staleness bug the heartbeat exists to close, just via a different trigger.

findings.title: Heartbeat join has a timeout but nothing checks whether the thread actually stopped before a terminal status is written, so a stalled write_status can still overwrite DONE/FAILED with RUNNING
findings.detail: `_heartbeat`'s finally clause does `stop.set(); thread.join(timeout=heartbeat_seconds() + 5)` (lines 258-261) and then returns control to `publish`, which returns to `ingest_archive.Command.handle`, which then runs `discard_staged`, removes the local temp file, and only then writes the terminal DONE/FAILED status (ingest_archive.py lines 79-88). None of that checks `thread.is_alive()` after the join. `write_status`/`_replace` (lines 111-163) perform an unbounded blocking I/O call (`backend.save` or `os.fdopen`/`os.replace`) with no timeout configured anywhere in this codebase's storage layer, so a slow or hung write (network stall to S3, a wedged local disk) can keep the heartbeat thread alive well past the join's timeout budget. The window between the join timing out and the process actually exiting (discard_staged I/O, file removal, the terminal write itself) is exactly where a straggling beat can finish its in-flight `write_status(state=RUNNING, ...)` call and land after the command's DONE/FAILED write -- putting a finished or failed job back to RUNNING, with nothing to detect or correct it. The docstring at lines 239-241 explicitly claims 'a beat already in flight has to land before the caller writes its terminal status', which the timeout-without-verification implementation does not actually guarantee.
findings.suggested_fix: After `thread.join(timeout=...)`, check `thread.is_alive()`. If still alive, log at error/critical level (this is now an anomaly, not routine) and either block until the thread truly exits before letting the caller write a terminal status, or have the terminal write path re-assert itself (e.g. write the terminal status again after confirming the thread is dead, or gate all writers behind a shared lock/generation counter so a stale RUNNING write from an old heartbeat can be detected and rejected).

findings.title: write_status failures are only logged, never counted or escalated -- a run of failed beats makes a live job look dead again with no signal
findings.detail: `write_status` (lines 111-123) swallows every exception with `except Exception: logger.warning(...)`, and the heartbeat loop (lines 249-252) calls it on a fixed cadence with no tracking of success/failure. If the backend is transiently unable to accept writes (expired credentials, a throttled bucket, a full local disk), every beat fails the same way, `updated` stops advancing, and `_fail_if_stale` (lines 187-213) will eventually report the job FAILED on the next poll even though the process is still running and may still complete and try to publish. This is the same class of false-staleness bug the heartbeat was built to close, just triggered by write failures instead of a long blocking stage, and this commit adds no counting, backoff, or escalation to distinguish 'briefly unlucky' from 'storage is down for this job'.
findings.suggested_fix: Track consecutive write_status failures inside the heartbeat loop (or have write_status return a success/failure signal the loop can inspect). After N consecutive failures, escalate beyond logger.warning (error/critical, or an operational alert) so a beating-but-can't-report job is distinguishable from one that has genuinely stopped, and so operators can catch storage outages before staleness silently misreports live jobs as failed.

findings.title: heartbeat_seconds() docstring's 'quarter of the window, three beats can be lost' claim doesn't describe the capped/floored behavior actually implemented
findings.detail: `heartbeat_seconds()` is `max(1.0, min(60.0, STALE_AFTER_SECONDS / 4))` (line 73). For the documented default (STALE_AFTER_SECONDS=1800), the cap dominates: the real beat interval is 60s, not 450s/4=112.5s and not the '3 lost beats' the docstring describes -- the actual tolerance is ~30 missed beats before staleness fires (safer than claimed, but the docstring is simply wrong about the margin for the shipped default). At the other end, for STALE_AFTER_SECONDS configured below ~4s the 1.0 floor can equal or exceed the stale window itself, meaning the real formula (not the test suite's monkeypatched override of heartbeat_seconds) could produce a beat interval as long as, or longer than, the window it is meant to keep ahead of. This only matters for unusually small NGIAB_JOB_STALE_SECONDS values, which is why confidence is capped at moderate.
findings.suggested_fix: Fix the docstring to describe the actual behavior once the cap/floor are applied for realistic configuration ranges, and consider clamping the floor relative to STALE_AFTER_SECONDS (e.g. heartbeat_seconds() should never exceed some fraction of STALE_AFTER_SECONDS even when the naive quarter would be below 1.0).

residual_risks: Between the subprocess being SIGKILLed and STALE_AFTER_SECONDS elapsing (default 30 minutes), the client still sees RUNNING with no narrower signal. This is unchanged by the commit and appears to be an accepted architectural tradeoff (nothing supervises the child process), not a regression -- flagged for visibility only.

The heartbeat and the stage-transition writes in publish/_run/ingest_archive.py are uncoordinated writers to the same status key with no locking or generation check; last-write-wins by wall-clock arrival order at the storage backend rather than by logical happens-before order, which is what makes finding P1 possible under slow I/O.
testing_gaps: No test simulates write_status/backend.save blocking or hanging long enough to exceed thread.join's timeout, so the ordering guarantee the docstring claims ('a beat already in flight has to land before the caller writes its terminal status') is never actually tested under the load/latency conditions where it could fail.

No test exercises persistent write_status failure (e.g. monkeypatching the storage backend to always raise) to confirm what a client observes when a live, beating job cannot successfully report -- specifically whether it incorrectly reads as FAILED via staleness despite the process being alive.

All heartbeat timing tests monkeypatch `ingest.heartbeat_seconds` directly rather than exercising the real formula through small STALE_AFTER_SECONDS values, so the 1.0s-floor-vs-tiny-window edge case in heartbeat_seconds() itself is untested.

No test verifies that the two writers (heartbeat vs. stage-transition/terminal writes) never race when both are triggered close together under real thread scheduling delays, rather than the deterministic, fast-clock scenario the fixtures set up.
